Of which Pygmalion, King of Tyre, will bear certain witness, who treacherously killed Sichaeus, his first cousin and the husband of Dido his sister, to make booty of his treasure and his goods <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>; Polymnestor also, King of Thrace, who by great treachery killed Polydorus, son of Priam (given into his keeping at the time of the Trojan war), to seize his gold and his silver <sup class="mk" data-key="d">d</sup>. And what is still more marvellous, Eriphyle, too covetous, spurred by I know not what goad to obtain the rich jewel that Adrastus, King of the Argives, had, dared to undertake to betray and disclose Amphiaraus her husband, who had hidden himself so as not to go to the war of Thebes, for fear of being killed there as had been foretold to him <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>. english.html: To what do you not drive mortal hearts, accursed hunger for gold?

That is why the Emperor Marcus Antoninus, a prince generous and excellent in every virtue, dreaded nothing in his life so much as the name and repute of an avaricious man, nor ever detested anything with such great vehemence as avarice, <sup class="mk" data-key="g">g</sup> mother, source and root of all evils <sup class="mk" data-key="h">h</sup>, and which, as Sallust says in some place, overturns faith, probity and every virtue <sup class="mk" data-key="i">i</sup>.

notes.citation: Julius Capitolinus, Life of Marcus Antoninus (Historia Augusta); chapter not located
notes.original: Iule Capito lin en la vie d'Antonin.
notes.gloss: Coras's "M. Antonin" is Marcus Aurelius; Capitolinus also wrote the life of Antoninus Pius, and the passage has not been located in either.
